summary: In the 1990s Merck rushed its painkiller Vioxx to market, buried evidence that it caused heart attacks and sold it with celebrity ads until its 2004 withdrawal, after it was linked to tens of thousands of US deaths.

evidence.note: MBA Raymond Gilmartin becomes Merck CEO in 1994 and launches the crash program for a COX-2 drug
1996 internal Merck study shows cardiovascular harm at high doses; company presses on
Merck ghostwrites trial papers under outside academics' names and drops heart attacks from data
FDA approves Vioxx in 1999 despite a reviewer's warning about cardiovascular events
paid Dorothy Hamill campaign from 2000, Larry King appearance and FDA objections
Groopman's 1998 New Yorker super-aspirin article quotes a conflicted FDA panelist
Pfizer-funded anesthesiologist Scott Reuben publishes fabricated COX-2 studies from 2000
Bob Ernst dies in 2001; widow's Texas suit wins a large verdict in 2005
Merck withdraws Vioxx in late September 2004 as lawsuits mount
press and pundits mock the Ernst verdict as a frivolous lawsuit, siding with Merck
30,000 suits, a settlement in 2008 and a misdemeanor guilty plea for misbranding
Reuben exposed in 2009 and sentenced in 2010 to prison and restitution

notes: Taxonomy lists Vioxx as a medical-malpractice example, but the harm came from a company's product and cover-up, so corporate-malfeasance is primary. Tylenol, aspirin and 1971-1992 COX research treated as background. Pfizer/Celebrex and Gilmartin kept as keywords to stay within five subjects. Closing talk on pharma distrust, COVID and RFK Jr. is commentary, so reaches_present is false. Reuben's birth year not given; floruit used.
